ideal_answer: Paging is a memory management scheme that eliminates the need for contiguous allocation of physical memory. This scheme permits the physical address space of a process to be non-contiguous. It uses page tables to translate logical addresses to physical addresses, avoiding external fragmentation.

A deadlock is a situation where a set of processes are blocked because each process is holding a resource and waiting for another resource held by some other process. The four necessary conditions are mutual exclusion, hold and wait, no preemption, and circular wait.

CPU scheduling is the process of selecting a process from the ready queue to execute on the CPU. It aims to maximize CPU utilization and throughput. Algorithms include FCFS, SJF, and Round Robin which uses time-sharing via a fixed time quantum.

Page replacement algorithms decide which memory page to swap out when a page fault occurs and physical memory is full. Examples include FIFO, which replaces the oldest page, and LRU, which replaces the least recently used page to minimize future page faults.

Virtual memory is a technique that allows the execution of processes that are not completely in main memory. It gives the illusion of a very large memory by using secondary storage (disk) as an extension of RAM, typically implemented via demand paging.
